cards.text: Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, receives a burden against Babylon. Get comfortable, friend. This message is HEAVY, and I'm a stamper on a solid gold base, so I know heavy.
It opens with orders. Raise a banner on a barren hilltop, call aloud to them, wave your hand.

cards.question: A banner goes up on a bare hilltop in this burden against Babylon, and hands start waving. What's the signal for?

answers.text: So they may enter the gates of the nobles
So they may leave the land in peace
So they may bring gifts to the king

cards.text: Then the LORD speaks for Himself: "I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors…"

cards.question: The LORD summons His warriors to carry out His ___.

cards.text: Then a noise. A tumult on the mountains, like a great multitude, and an uproar among the kingdoms, like nations gathered together. That's LOUDER than the dead batteries I shared a drawer with, arguing over who had the most charge left.

cards.question: All that uproar on the mountains and among the kingdoms. What's causing it?

answers.text: The LORD of Hosts raising an army
The kings of Egypt making a treaty
The tribes of Israel coming home

cards.question: The army the LORD is gathering comes from close by, just over the nearest hill.

cards.text: They're coming from faraway lands, from the ends of the heavens, to destroy the whole country. Then the cry goes out: wail, because the Day of the LORD is near.

cards.question: Isaiah says the Day of the LORD will come as ___ from the Almighty.
When the Day of the LORD comes, all hands fall limp. What happens to every man's heart?

cards.text: Terror, pain and anguish seize them. They look at one another, their faces flushed with fear.

cards.question: Isaiah compares the way these terrified people writhe to someone. Who?

cards.text: Behold, the Day of the LORD is coming, cruel, with fury and burning anger. It comes to make the earth a desolation.

cards.question: The Day of the LORD comes to make the earth a desolation. Who does it destroy within it?

cards.text: Then the lights start going out. The stars of heaven and their constellations won't give their light, and friend, I light stars for a living, so that one hits me right in the apron.

cards.question: On the Day of the LORD, the rising sun will be darkened, but the moon will still give its light.

cards.text: The LORD keeps speaking: "I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity."

cards.question: The LORD says He'll punish the wicked. Who else does He say He'll bring low?

cards.text: Next, the LORD talks about gold. Not just any gold, the gold of Ophir. And as a guy who once sold for 25 cents, I am NOT the expert on precious things.

cards.question: The LORD says He'll make man scarcer than pure gold, rarer than the gold of Ophir. What's that picture saying?

answers.text: Very few people will be left
Gold will run out in the land

cards.text: The heavens tremble, and the earth is shaken from its place. And the people scatter like a hunted gazelle, like a sheep without a shepherd.

cards.question: Scattered like a sheep without a shepherd, where does each person run?

answers.text: Up into the caves to hide

cards.text: Isaiah doesn't soften this part, friend. Whoever is caught dies by the sword, houses are looted, and families suffer terribly.

cards.question: God says He'll stir up the Medes, a nation, against them. True or false: the Medes can be bought off with silver and gold.

cards.text: The Medes have no regard for silver and no desire for gold. They're like my oven timer, friend. You can NOT negotiate with it. I have tried. It does not care.
Their bows show no mercy, not even to the children. Then Isaiah names the city: Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, Babylon's people.

cards.question: Isaiah says Babylon will be overthrown by God like two other cities. Which two?
After Babylon is overthrown, a later generation will move back in and settle there again.

cards.text: Never inhabited, from generation to generation. Not even a nomad pitches his tent there, and no shepherd rests his flock there.

cards.question: No people settle in Babylon after it falls. So who moves into her houses?

cards.text: Hyenas howl in her fortresses, and jackals in her luxurious palaces. The jewel of the kingdoms just became the WORST rental listing you have ever seen.

cards.question: Isaiah ends with one more word about Babylon's time. How close does he say it is?

findings.problem: The joke calls Papa Dorin's base 'solid gold.' His world only gives him a 'gold base.' Making it solid gold adds a new fact to his world.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: Card 2 stops the line at 'wave your hand.' The right answer, 'So they may enter the gates of the nobles,' is just the rest of that line almost word for word. The baker has to guess the next words of a prophetic line instead of reasoning about what it means.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This story card only repeats the answer to card 8 (the Medes have no regard for silver and no desire for gold) and adds a joke. It doesn't move the passage forward. Verse 18 comes on the next card.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: The question asks who moves 'into her houses,' but Isaiah 13:21 says the howling creatures fill her houses. The desert creatures 'lie down there' and the wild goats 'leap about.' The text never puts either group in her houses, so the right answer isn't true for both groups as the question is worded.

rule.text: A card about two groups needs an answer true for both. When a question covers more than one group, like the sea creatures and the birds, the right answer must be true for every group in it.

findings.problem: 'The jewel of the kingdoms just became the WORST rental listing' says the desolation has already happened, and just now. Isaiah 13:21-22 says it 'will' happen and that Babylon's time 'is at hand.' The joke adds a time the text doesn't give.

rule.text: Times stay true. No time in the text means none added.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has 8 choice cards: 6 multiple choice, 2 true or false and no fill in the blank. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Isaiah 13:16 describes infants dashed to pieces and wives ravished. The card says 'families suffer terribly,' right after saying 'Isaiah doesn't soften this part.' So the card softens the text while saying the text isn't softened. The docs say the content is for adults and must be 'always clean,' and that things are called what the text calls them, but they don't say how to handle graphic violence or sexual violence in Scripture.
findings.question: For graphic violence or sexual violence in a passage, like Isaiah 13:16, should Prep name what the text says, use a gentler summary, or leave it to the reveal screen? If it uses a summary, should the lead-in line ('doesn't soften this part') be dropped?

findings.problem: Many story cards tell this future-tense prophecy in the present tense: 'Terror, pain and anguish seize them,' 'The heavens tremble,' 'Hyenas howl in her fortresses.' That can make a prophecy sound like something happening now or already done. The docs don't say what tense to use when retelling prophecy.
findings.question: When Prep retells a prophecy written in the future tense ('will'), may Papa Dorin tell it in the present tense like a story, or should he keep the future tense ('will')?
